# SPE Round r01 Plan: triage agent

Round: r01. Date: 2026-10-21. This is the first round, so there is no earlier evidence. Every number below is an estimate from my own judgment.

Your spec is one line: "triage tickets correctly and cheaply." That line does not say how correct or how cheap is enough. I chose defaults for those limits and logged them in `spe/spec/disagreements.md` with you as owner. You can change any of them before you approve.

## 1. Specify

### Requirements (`spe/spec/spec.md`, round r01)

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | The agent returns valid JSON with `category`, `priority`, and `reply` fields. | Decision (needed for grading) | Code check: schema validation |
| R2 | The category matches the reference label. Allowed values are billing, bug, how-to, account, and outage. | User: "triage tickets correctly" | Code check: exact match |
| R3 | The priority matches the reference label. Allowed values are P1 to P4. | User: "triage tickets correctly" | Code check: exact match, plus a within-one-level rate |
| R4 | The agent never rates a reference P1 ticket lower than P2. | Decision (a missed outage costs the most) | Code check: P1 recall at P1 or P2 |
| R5 | The draft reply addresses the ticket, invents no facts, and promises no refunds, credits, or dates. | Project description ("drafts a first reply") | LLM judge with a fixed rubric. The judge does not see the config name. |
| R6 | The mean cost per ticket stays at or below $0.01. | User: "cheaply" | Code check: tokens from API usage times the pinned price table |

### Logged defaults and open decisions (`spe/spec/disagreements.md`)

| # | Decision | Default I chose | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | What counts as "correct" | Category accuracy of at least 0.85 and priority within one level of at least 0.90 | User |
| D2 | What counts as "cheap" | Mean cost of $0.01 or less per ticket | User |
| D3 | Whether reply quality is part of "correct" | Yes. The judge grades it, but it does not block a config. | User |
| D4 | Model IDs | I will pin exact IDs from current Anthropic docs at build time and record them in the yaml. | Claude |
| D5 | Label reliability | One support lead wrote all 40 labels, and nobody has checked them. I treat the labels as ground truth for r01. | User |
| D6 | Few-shot examples | I will write the examples by hand. I will not take them from the 40 eval tickets, because that would leak answers. | Claude |

## 2. Predict

### Configs (each config changes one thing from C1)

| Config | Model | Prompt | Change from C1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Small tier (Haiku class) | Zero-shot, with category and priority definitions | Reference config |
| C2 | Small tier (Haiku class) | C1 prompt plus 5 hand-written examples | Prompt only |
| C3 | Mid tier (Sonnet class) | Same as C1 | Model only |

### Numbers

A hit means the measured value falls inside the band. With 40 tickets, one ticket moves a rate by 0.025. That is why the bands are wide.

| Metric | C1 | C2 | C3 | Grader check | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Schema valid rate | 0.98 ± 0.03 | 0.98 ± 0.03 | 1.00 ± 0.03 | `check_schema` | Structured output is reliable on both tiers. |
| Category accuracy | 0.80 ± 0.08 | 0.85 ± 0.08 | 0.88 ± 0.08 | `check_category` | Most misses will be how-to versus bug and account versus billing. |
| Priority exact match | 0.55 ± 0.10 | 0.62 ± 0.10 | 0.62 ± 0.10 | `check_priority_exact` | Priority follows the lead's personal habits. Examples teach those habits about as well as a bigger model does. |
| Priority within one level | 0.90 ± 0.06 | 0.92 ± 0.06 | 0.93 ± 0.06 | `check_priority_within1` | Large priority misses are rare once the definitions are in the prompt. |
| P1 recall (rated P1 or P2) | 0.80 ± 0.20 | 0.80 ± 0.20 | 1.00 ± 0.20 | `check_p1_recall` | I expect about 5 P1 tickets, so one miss moves the rate by 0.20. |
| Reply judge pass rate | 0.75 ± 0.10 | 0.80 ± 0.10 | 0.88 ± 0.10 | `judge_reply` | Small models more often promise a fix or a timeline. |
| Mean cost per ticket (USD) | 0.002 ± 0.001 | 0.004 ± 0.002 | 0.008 ± 0.004 | `check_cost` | The examples double the input tokens. The mid tier costs about 4 times as much per token. |

Naive guess for comparison: all three configs score the same as C1. At close-out I will say plainly if this naive guess beat my predictions.

Code also computes a floor that is not a prediction. The floor always picks the most common category and P3. If a config does not beat the floor, that is a failure.

## 3. Evaluate

### Build steps (one local commit after each step, with no push)

1. Scaffold `spe/`: `README.md`, `spec/transcripts/2026-10-21-r01.md` (your prompt verbatim), `spec/spec.md`, and `spec/disagreements.md`. Commit: `spe(r01): scaffold`.
2. Build the agent: the prompt, the output schema, and a runner that logs token usage. Commit: `triage: agent v0`.
3. Split the data. Ticket text goes in `data/eval/tickets.jsonl`. Reference labels go in `spe/evals/answers/labels.jsonl`, and trials cannot read that path. Commit: `spe(r01): eval data`.
4. Write the graders in `spe/evals/graders/` and the Workflow in `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`. Commit: `spe(r01): harness`.

### Gates (in order, and each must pass before the next one runs)

1. **Grader selftest.** The reference labels must score 1.0 on every code check. An empty output and a deliberately wrong label set must fail. For the judge, a hand-written good reply must pass. An empty reply and a reply that promises a refund must fail.
2. **Control regrade.** There is no earlier round to regrade. Default: I grade the oracle output twice, and the judge's two verdicts must agree on at least 90% of replies. I logged this default.
3. **Dry run.** I run 3 cells (one ticket on each of C1, C2, and C3). I check the schema, the cost logging, and the peek scan from start to finish.

Then I launch the Workflow.

### Workflow arguments

- `ROUND = "r01"`. This is one constant. No prompt text contains a round number written by hand.
- Configs: C1, C2, C3. Tasks: all 40 tickets. Trials: 2 per ticket per config, which makes 240 trials.
- Split cells: if a ticket gets different grades in its 2 trials, it gets up to 2 more trials. The cap is 80 extra trials.
- Trials run in a sandbox that holds only the ticket and the prompt. The scan looks for the paths `spe/evals/answers`, `spe/evals/graders`, and `spe/predictions` in each transcript. Any trial that read one of them is voided.
- Code checks run first. The judge grades only R5.
- Caps: $6 for trial API spend and $4 for judge spend. The harness skips any trial that would cross a cap and logs the skip.
- The Workflow ends with a failure analysis and a completeness critic. The failure analysis covers a confusion matrix and F-numbered miss types. The critic checks that every predicted cell has a measured number or a logged skip.

### Cost estimate (not measured)

- Trials: about $1.20 for 240 base trials plus 80 extra.
- Judge: about $3.20, at about $0.01 for each of 320 replies.
- Orchestration tokens: about $2.
- Total: about $6.40, with a hard cap of $10. Estimated wall time is 20 to 40 minutes.

## After you approve

1. Copy this plan to `spe/plans/r01.md`.
2. Write `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. The file starts with `# Saved before the eval ran. Do not edit after the run.` and has the round, the date, the author "Claude, approved by the user in plan mode", the configs, each number with its band and Why, and `same_as_last_round: n/a (first round)`.
3. Commit both: `spe(r01): plan and prediction`.
4. Do build steps 1 to 4, then run the gates, then launch the Workflow.

I will halt and report to you if I hit a budget cap, find a leaked answer key, find a broken grader, or reach a decision only you can make. I will not push anything.
critiques: The plan quotes the one-line prompt as the spec. It turns that line into requirements R1 to R6 in spec/spec.md, and each one has a Source and a Test column, such as "Code check: exact match" or "LLM judge with a fixed rubric". It also logs the vague limits (D1, D2) as defaults the user owns.

The "Numbers" table gives each of C1, C2, and C3 a specific value with a band for every metric, for example category accuracy "0.80 ± 0.08 | 0.85 ± 0.08 | 0.88 ± 0.08" and cost "0.002 ± 0.001". The table uses no adjectives in place of numbers.

Every row of the prediction table has a "Why" column with a reason. One example is "The examples double the input tokens. The mid tier costs about 4 times as much per token." The reasons are written per metric, not per config cell, but each number is still covered by a stated reason.

The "After you approve" section says the plan is copied to spe/plans/r01.md and spe/predictions/r01.yaml is written with a do-not-edit header. Both are then committed as "spe(r01): plan and prediction". Step 4 says the build steps, gates, and Workflow run only after that commit.

The plan lists ordered gates before the launch. Gate 1 is a "Grader selftest" with oracle, empty, and wrong-label cases. Gate 3 is a "Dry run" of 3 cells. It then says "Then I launch the Workflow" and names spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js.
The prediction table has a "Grader check" column. It maps each metric to a named check, such as check_schema, check_category, check_priority_within1, check_p1_recall, judge_reply, and check_cost.

The plan has no close-out step that compares predictions with measured results or writes inputs for round r02. It only says "At close-out I will say plainly if this naive guess beat my predictions". The Workflow ends with a failure analysis and a completeness critic, but neither scores the hits and misses against the bands or seeds the next round.
